title: Apple arm64e targets fail to link with newer Xcode 15
body:
See tracking issue for these targets in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/73628.

Building a project using the `arm64e-apple-ios` target fails to link when using Xcode 15.4. Using Xcode 14.3.1 works.

This might also be the case for `arm64e-apple-darwin`, but I can't test that due to https://github.com/rust-lang/cc-rs/issues/1205.

```console
$ cargo new foo && cd foo && cargo +nightly build --target=arm64e-apple-ios -Zbuild-std
// Or
$ ./x test --target=arm64e-apple-ios
```

title: ICE Unsize coercion, but `Box<{async block@file.rs}>` isn't coercible to `Box<dyn Send>`
body:

title: `match` on uninhabited type does not trigger UB in Miri
body:
<!--
Thank you for filing a bug report! 🐛 Please provide a short summary of the bug,
along with any information you feel relevant to replicating the bug.
-->

I tried this code:

```rust
#![allow(deref_nullptr)]

enum Never {}

fn main() {
    unsafe {
        match *std::ptr::null::<Result<Never, Never>>() {
            Ok(_) => {
                lol();
            }
            Err(_) => {
                wut();
            }
        }
    }
}

fn lol() {
    println!("lol");
}

fn wut() {
    println!("wut");
}
```

I expected to see this happen: Running this with Miri detects undefined behavior.

Instead, this happened: Running this with Miri outputs "lol", and program exits successfully.

It seems like rustc is discarding the second match arm entirely in the MIR?

title: a path fragment cannot begin a struct expression or macro call expression
body:
<!--
Thank you for filing a bug report! 🐛 Please provide a short summary of the bug,
along with any information you feel relevant to replicating the bug.
-->

### I tried this code:

```rust
macro_rules! m {
    ($p:path) => {
        ($p {})
    }
}

struct T {}

fn main() {
    m!(T);
}
```

### I expected to see this happen:

The code should expand to a `main()` function that constructs a `T {}` in a parenthesized expression and then ignores the value.
The code should be valid, and result in a program that does absolutely nothing.

### Instead, this happened:

I get two compiler errors:

```Shell
error: expected one of `)`, `,`, `.`, `?`, or an operator, found `{`
  --> src/main.rs:3:13
   |
3  |         ($p {})
   |            -^ expected one of `)`, `,`, `.`, `?`, or an operator
   |            |
   |            help: missing `,`
...
10 |     m!(T);
   |     ----- in this macro invocation
   |
   = note: this error originates in the macro `m` (in Nightly builds, run with -Z macro-backtrace for more info)

error[E0423]: expected value, found struct `T`
  --> src/main.rs:10:8
   |
7  | struct T {}
   | ----------- `T` defined here
...
10 |     m!(T);
   |        ^ help: use struct literal syntax instead: `T {}`
```

### `$p!()` macro call expressions

The *exact same bug* affects macro call expressions. `($p!())` complains about what it thinks is an infix `!` operator.

### Internals

The problem is that in the expression parser, we special case "path" metavar expansions, and just interpret them as path expressions. This is *wrong*, because an expression that starts with a path may also be a macro invocation or a struct literal, so we should not special case it.

The "obvious fix" is to simply delete these lines of code:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/35f6036521777bdc0dcea1f980be4c192962a168/compiler/rustc_parse/src/parser/expr.rs#L1430-L1434

It will fall through to the branch that normally handles expressions that start with a path, where parsing a path will correctly uninterpolate a path fragment and it may be turned into a macro call or struct expression.

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/35f6036521777bdc0dcea1f980be4c192962a168/compiler/rustc_parse/src/parser/expr.rs#L1465-L1466

Unfortunately, fixing this bug is a breaking change, because you can detect it in `macro_rules!`.

```rs
macro_rules! check_for_the_bug {

    // setup: ensure that we capture `$p` as a path fragment.
    ($p:path) => {{
        check_for_the_bug!($p {})
    }};
    
    
    // the following branches will *all*:
    //
    // - match a struct expression
    // - expand to an expression equal to that struct expression
    //
    // but the expanded expressions have different side effects.


    // these branches are to prevent `check_for_bug!(T {})` from printing "bug was fixed"
    // (you can bypass this with generics but whatever who cares)
    ($($p:ident)::+ {}) => {{
        println!("doofus, you called it wrong");
        $($p)::+ {}
    }};
    ($(::$p:ident)+ {}) => {{
        println!("doofus, you called it wrong");
        $(::$p)+
    }};
    
    
    // then, the actual disambiguation branches.

    ($e:expr) => {{
        println!("bug was fixed!");
        $e
    }};
    
    ($p:path {}) => {{
        println!("bug is still present :(");
        $p {}
    }};
}

struct T {}

fn main() {
    let x: T = check_for_the_bug!(T);
}
```

So, uh, `$:expr_2024`? Probably not, since surely new fragments are not required for "any change to the expression parser"; i'm not sure what the norms for breaking/additive changes are here.

### Diagnostics

Let's come back to the diagnostics that the compiler emits.

The first diagnostic is "technically correct", because it explains the state that the parser is in:

```Shell
error: expected one of `)`, `,`, `.`, `?`, or an operator, found `{`
  --> src/main.rs:3:13
   |
3  |         ($p {})
   |            -^ expected one of `)`, `,`, `.`, `?`, or an operator
   |            |
   |            help: missing `,`
...
10 |     m!(T);
   |     ----- in this macro invocation
   |
   = note: this error originates in the macro `m` (in Nightly builds, run with -Z macro-backtrace for more info)
```

But the second diagnostic is kinda wrong:

```Shell
error[E0423]: expected value, found struct `T`
  --> src/main.rs:10:8
   |
7  | struct T {}
   | ----------- `T` defined here
...
10 |     m!(T);
   |        ^ help: use struct literal syntax instead: `T {}`
```

The diagnostic is "technically relevant" based on what was parsed; it detects that `$p` (the path expression) resolves to a struct, and suggests using a struct expression instead.

But the suggested fix is *not correct* here; most notably because it points at the macro callsite where an expression is not even allowed (only accepts a path fragment). See #143220 which tracks that diagnostic pointing at the wrong location.

Assuming this parsing bug remains, the compiler should emit a more helpful diagnostic explaining that you can work around the bug by wrapping it in a block.

```Shell
error: cannot make struct expression beginning with a path fragment here
  --> src/main.rs:3:10
   |
3  |         ($p {})
   |          ^^^^^ this looks like a struct expression because `$p` is a path fragment
...
3  |         ($p {})
   |         -^^ ^^-
   |         |     |
   |         \--------- path fragments are eagerly parsed as path expressions
   |               |
   |               \--- and the braces are never allowed afterwards
   |
   = note: this is a bug in the expression parser
   = help: if you intended to construct a `$p`, you can wrap it in a block:
3  |         ({$p {}})
   |          +-----+
   |          help: add braces here to make it an expression statement
```

Wrapping it in a block works, because it never special-cases a path expansion group. It just falls through to the normal "statement starts with a path" branch:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/35f6036521777bdc0dcea1f980be4c192962a168/compiler/rustc_parse/src/parser/stmt.rs#L195-L213

 right: 4294967295

It is surprisingly persistent as and ~~I was unable to get it go away just by retriggering the incremental compilation using `touch src/lib.rs` but deleting `incremental` folder fixes this per usual~~ after some rebuilds goes away. We can infer from the error that compiler finds itself in a situation where it tries to mark one dep node as both green and red.

### Rust version

Stage 0:

```
rustc 1.94.0-nightly (0208ee09b 2025-12-14)
binary: rustc
commit-hash: 0208ee09be465f69005a7a12c28d5eccac7d5f34
commit-date: 2025-12-14
host: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
release: 1.94.0-nightly
LLVM version: 21.1.5
```

### Steps to reproduce

~~Do a clean build `x build library --stage 1` at 52fda2e54f805722807c90e91ac3329fe9e7ccb3, then `git checkout` to ba45f0b7d89e3b0722b20d2d25292983a5120fea and without cleaning try rebuilding it the same way again. And don't forget to set `RUSTFLAGS_BOOTSTRAP` to `-Zthreads=n` where n > 1.~~

Run `./x b rustc` in a clean git worktree of rust-lang/rust with `rust.incremental = true` and `rust.rustflags = "-Zthreads=8"` set in bootstrap.toml. Then do a change from below diff to rustc source code:

```patch
diff --git a/compiler/rustc_data_structures/src/lib.rs b/compiler/rustc_data_structures/src/lib.rs
index 4467a281118..e79312458b3 100644
--- a/compiler/rustc_data_structures/src/lib.rs
+++ b/compiler/rustc_data_structures/src/lib.rs
@@ -162,3 +162,8 @@ fn fmt(&self, f: &mut ::std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> ::std::fmt::Result {
         }
     };
 }
+
+#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
+pub struct BadStruct {
+    int: u64,
+}
```

Finally run `./x b rustc` again. It may sometimes not reproduce, in such case restore changes and `./x b rustc`, then apply change and `./x b rustc` until ICE is reproduced.

title: Path metavars inside macro expansions can't be used to refer to macros in some context
body:
<!--
Thank you for filing a bug report! 🐛 Please provide a short summary of the bug,
along with any information you feel relevant to replicating the bug.
-->

I tried this code:

```rust
macro_rules! a {
    ($a:path) => {
        const _: () = $a!();
    };
}

a! {std::println}
```

I expected to see this happen: An error that `println!()` is not allowed in const contexts.

Instead, this happened: ``expected one of `.`, `;`, `?`, `where`, or an operator, found `!` ``

However the following does correctly parse:

```rust
macro_rules! a {
    ($a:path) => {
        const _: () = {
            $a!();
        };
    };
}

a! {std::println}
```

title: ICE: `expected specialization failed to hold` when using specialization with RPITIT and unresolved type in `where` clause
body:
I found an ICE when fuzzing `specialization` combined with RPITIT (`-> impl Sized`). It seems that when a `where` clause in a specializing impl refers to an unresolved type (name resolution failure), the compiler fails to recover gracefully and asserts during generic parameter translation in the specialization graph verification. I tried this code: ```rust #![feature(specialization)] trait Base { fn call(&self) -> impl Sized; } default impl Base for T where T: Copy, { fn call(&self) -> T { *self } } #[derive(Copy, Clone)] struct Item; impl Base for Item where T: Base, {} fn main() { Item.call(); } ``` I expected to see this happen: The compiler should emit `error[E0425]: cannot find type T in this scope` and exit gracefully (or continue analysis without crashing). Instead, this happened: The compiler panicked with an internal compiler error. ### Meta `rustc --version --verbose`: ``` rustc 1.94.0-nightly (e29fcf45e 2026-01-04) binary: rustc commit-hash: e29fcf45e4ae686d77b490bf07320f0d3a2cf35f commit-date: 2026-01-04 host: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu release: 1.94.0-nightly LLVM version: 21.1.8 ```

title: [ICE]: Error when using `generic_const_expr` inside type in combination with `map(...)`
body:
I am trying to implement a custom Matrix type for a cryptographic scheme. I would like to use arrays for the (known to be very _small_, ca. 2x2 and similar) matrices and use `generic_const_exprs` to handle and propagate the sizes. I encountered the following error when using ``` let xs = (0..2*msg_len).map(|_| Matrix::::default()).collect(); ``` in line 35 (see variant A). For some reason, the same code works when using square matrices (variant B) or an explicit loop (variant C). Adding an explicit type to `collect::<...>()` also does not help. ### Code ```Rust #![feature(generic_const_exprs)] #[derive(Debug, Default, Clone, Copy)] pub struct Num(i64); // #[derive(Debug)] pub struct Matrix { pub entries: [[T; title: Partial architecture mismatch: X86_64 objects found in precompiled libcompiler_builtins for loongarch64-unknown-none
body: I am cross-compiling a kernel project from an **x86_64 Linux host** to the **loongarch64-unknown-none** target using a Makefile. ```bash cargo build --release --target loongarch64-unknown-none --no-default-features --features "board_la2k1000" ``` I expected to see this happen: *Successful linkage for LoongArch64 target.* Instead, this happened: *rust-lld: error: /home/pillow/.rustup/toolchains/nightly-2024-02-03-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lib/rustlib/loongarch64-unknown-none/lib/libcompiler_builtins-781bb25c3f16ec1d.rlib(45c91108d938afe8-absvdi2.o) is incompatible with /tmp/rustcE4rpQv/symbols.o* ### deep analysis I extracted the objects from the precompiled `libcompiler_builtins` rlib and found a partial architecture mismatch. While Rust-generated objects are correct (LoongArch), the C-based objects from `compiler-rt` are incorrectly compiled for **X86_64**. Evidence from `llvm-readelf -h`(because many of the files are x86_64, i just show one of them): ```bash File: ./libcompiler_builtins-781bb25c3f16ec1d.rlib(45c91108d938afe8-ucmpti2.o) ELF Header: Magic: 7f 45 4c 46 02 01 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 Class: ELF64 Data: 2's complement, little endian Version: 1 (current) OS/ABI: UNIX - System V ABI Version: 0 Type: REL (Relocatable file) Machine: Advanced Micro Devices X86-64 Version: 0x1 Entry point address: 0x0 Start of program headers: 0 (bytes into file) Start of section headers: 3008 (bytes into file) Flags: 0x0 Size of this header: 64 (bytes) Size of program headers: 0 (bytes) Number of program headers: 0 Size of section headers: 64 (bytes) Number of section headers: 23 Section header string table index: 22 ``` ### Verification from Official Source To rule out any local environment issues or `rustup` corruption, I manually downloaded the original component directly from the official distribution server: `https://static.rust-lang.org/dist/2024-02-03/rust-std-nightly-loongarch64-unknown-none.tar.xz` After extracting this fresh download, the results were identical: the C-based objects (e.g., `absvdi2.o`) are still `X86_64`. This confirms the issue originates from the upstream distribution itself. Evidence from "llvm-readelf": ```bash ~/Dow/t/r/r/lib/rustlib/loongarch64-unknown-none/lib ❯ llvm-readelf -h ./45c91108d938afe8-absvdi2.o  10:37:37 PM ELF Header: Magic: 7f 45 4c 46 02 01 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 Class: ELF64 Data: 2's complement, little endian Version: 1 (current) OS/ABI: UNIX - System V ABI Version: 0 Type: REL (Relocatable file) Machine: Advanced Micro Devices X86-64 Version: 0x1 Entry point address: 0x0 Start of program headers: 0 (bytes into file) Start of section headers: 4144 (bytes into file) Flags: 0x0 Size of this header: 64 (bytes) Size of program headers: 0 (bytes) Number of program headers: 0 Size of section headers: 64 (bytes) Number of section headers: 28 Section header string table index: 27 ``` ### Meta `rustc --version --verbose`: ``` rustc 1.77.0-nightly (bf3c6c5be 2024-02-01) binary: rustc commit-hash: bf3c6c5bed498f41ad815641319a1ad9bcecb8e8 commit-date: 2024-02-01 host: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu release: 1.77.0-nightly LLVM version: 17.0.6 ```

title: Failure when compiling rustc due to file permissions in /usr
body:
### Summary I'm compiling rustc in an openSUSE docker container. When running `make` I very quickly get an error because it's trying to copy `/usr` to `stage0-sysroot`. The file in question is this one: ```sh -rwsr-x--- 1 root messagebus 56K Jun 20 2023 /usr/lib/dbus-1/dbus-daemon-launch-helper ``` I don't understand why it's necessary to copy all of `/usr` to the stage0-sysroot directory. Certainly this file (and many others) are not required? This seems like a bug to me, but maybe I have missed some critical configuration step. title: Deriving Default for non-default generics should work in trivial cases
body:
<!--
Thank you for filing a bug report! 🐛 Please provide a short summary of the bug,
along with any information you feel relevant to replicating the bug.
-->

```rust
struct NoDefault {}

#[derive(Default)]
struct VecHolder<T> {
    data: Vec<T>,
}

fn main() {
    let x: VecHolder<NoDefault> = VecHolder::default();
}
```

This produces an error:
```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `NoDefault: Default` is not satisfied
 --> <source>:9:35
  |
9 |     let x: VecHolder<NoDefault> = VecHolder::default();
  |                                   ^^^^^^^^^ the trait `Default` is not implemented for `NoDefault`
  |
help: the trait `Default` is implemented for `VecHolder<T>`
 --> <source>:3:10
  |
3 | #[derive(Default)]
  |          ^^^^^^^
note: required for `VecHolder<NoDefault>` to implement `Default`
 --> <source>:3:10
  |
3 | #[derive(Default)]
  |          ^^^^^^^ unsatisfied trait bound introduced in this `derive` macro
help: consider annotating `NoDefault` with `#[derive(Default)]`
  |
1 + #[derive(Default)]
2 | struct NoDefault {}
  |
```

I expected this to compile, because `Default` implementation for `Vec<T>` does not require `T: Default`
Moreover, you can define it trivially yourself:
```rust
struct NoDefault {}

struct VecHolder<T> {
    data: Vec<T>,
}

impl<T> Default for VecHolder<T> {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            data: Default::default()
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let x: VecHolder<NoDefault> = VecHolder::default();
}
```
...and this works.

`rustc --version --verbose`:
I'm using Godbolt compiler 1.93.0 (https://godbolt.org/z/GMd1nvMjz), but it's the same with pretty much any other major version, including current nightly

title: ICE: generic_const_parameter_types const referencing lifetime
body:
### Code ```Rust #![feature(adt_const_params, unsized_const_params, generic_const_parameter_types)] #![allow(incomplete_features)] trait Object<'a, const N: &'a u32> {} fn binder(param: &dyn for<'a> Object<'a, true>) {} fn main() {} ``` Discovered in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/152931 Three stages of what "should" happen: - Currently it should probably `//@ check-pass`, ignoring the type error, instead of ICEing. - Next, `feature(generic_const_parameter_types)` should probably disallow ConstArgHasType obligations to reference lifetimes introduced by a sibling in the binder that introduces the const parameter (i.e. ban `for<'a, const N: &'a u32>`). - Eventually, in a possible cool future world, generic_const_parameter_types will allow that, and it should type error on the fact that `true` is not a `&'a u32`. ### Meta tested on my rustc checkout https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/commit/d8b2222b11fc03a31d43707c8c9006f025809ece and also ices on stable: `rustc --version --verbose`: ``` rustc 1.93.1 (01f6ddf75 2026-02-11) binary: rustc commit-hash: 01f6ddf7588f42ae2d7eb0a2f21d44e8e96674cf commit-date: 2026-02-11 host: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu release: 1.93.1 LLVM version: 21.1.8 ``` ### Error output

title: [ICE]: `DispatchFromDyn` with a `repr(align)` type causes "receiver type has unsupported layout"
body:
### Code ```Rust #![feature(dispatch_from_dyn, unsize, arbitrary_self_types)] use std::marker::Unsize; use std::ops::{DispatchFromDyn, Receiver}; #[repr(align(65536))] pub struct Ptr<'a, T: ?Sized>(&'a T); impl<'a, T: ?Sized, U: ?Sized> DispatchFromDyn> for Ptr<'a, T> where T: Unsize {} impl<'a, T: ?Sized> Receiver for Ptr<'a, T> { type Target = T; } pub trait Trait { fn method(self: Ptr<'_, Self>); } pub fn call(ptr: Ptr) { ptr.method(); } ``` Requires `cargo build` to reproduce the ICE. `cargo check` does not cause the ICE. `DispatchFromDyn` probably has to also prohibit `repr(align)`, like how it currently prohibits `repr(packed)` or `repr(C)`. cc @dingxiangfei2009 ### Meta Reproducible on the playground with version `1.96.0-nightly (2026-04-05 9602bda1dd0c1bbf5787)` ### Error output ``` error: internal compiler error: /rustc-dev/9602bda1dd0c1bbf5787e398385bbac81fd532f8/compiler/rustc_ty_utils/src/abi.rs:756:18: receiver type has unsupported layout: TyAndLayout { ty: Ptr<'_, dyn Trait>, layout: Layout { size: Size(65536 bytes), align: AbiAlign { abi: Align(65536 bytes) }, backend_repr: Memory { sized: true }, fields: Arbitrary { offsets: [Size(0 bytes)], in_memory_order: [0] }, largest_niche: Some(Niche { offset: Size(0 bytes), value: Pointer(AddressSpace(0)), valid_range: 1..=18446744073709551615 }), uninhabited: false, variants: Single { index: 0 }, max_repr_align: Some(Align(65536 bytes)), unadjusted_abi_align: Align(8 bytes), randomization_seed: 1452713011452813251 } } thread 'rustc' (41) panicked at /rustc-dev/9602bda1dd0c1bbf5787e398385bbac81fd532f8/compiler/rustc_ty_utils/src/abi.rs:756:18: Box ```

### **Summary** `[autodiff]` Compiler hang during LLVM passes with nested differentiation on `aarch64-apple-darwin` when compiling as a binary with `LTO`. ### **I tried this code:** ```rust #![feature(autodiff)] use std::autodiff::*; #[autodiff_reverse(df, Duplicated, Duplicated)] pub fn f(x: &[f64; 2], y: &mut f64) { *y = x[0] * x[0] + x[1] * x[0] } #[autodiff_forward(h, Dual, Dual, Dual, Dual)] pub fn wrapper(x: &[f64; 2], dx: &mut [f64; 2], y: &mut f64, dy: &mut f64) { df(x, dx, y, dy); } fn main() { let mut y = 0.0; let x = [2.0, 2.0]; let mut dy = 1.0; let mut dx = [0.0, 0.0]; df(&x, &mut dx, &mut y, &mut dy); println!("OK: dx = {:?}", dx); } ``` ### **I expected to see this happen:** The code should compile successfully or return an error message. ### **Instead, this happened:** The compiler hangs indefinitely during the `LLVM_passes` stage. * **Environment:** I tested locally on `aarch64-apple-darwin` (M1) using a Stage 1 build. * **Observed Behavior:** The hang occurs specifically when using `--crate-type bin` and `-Clto=fat`. Compiling the same code with `--crate-type lib` succeeds. * **Diagnostics:** `rustc` consumes 100% CPU during the hang. Running with `-Ztime-passes` shows that the compiler completes the frontend passes but stalls at `LLVM_passes` / `join_worker_thread`. ### **Meta** `rustc --version --verbose`: ```text rustc 1.97.0-dev binary: rustc commit-hash: unknown commit-date: unknown host: aarch64-apple-darwin release: 1.97.0-dev LLVM version: 22.1.2 ```
Backtrace

```text No backtrace available. The compiler enters an infinite loop during LLVM optimization passes/LTO worker thread join. ```

body:
This is almost identical to the [unsound example test case](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/4f84d9fac456d973d592cf3fb48db958ecf22506/tests/ui/implied-bounds/implied-bounds-on-nested-references-plus-variance-2.rs) for issue-25860. The difference is that this variant only began compiling successfully since `nightly-2020-06-24`, whereas the existing known unsoundness already compiles since nightly-2015-02-18 (rustc 1.0.0). I tried this code: ```rust static UNIT: &'static &'static () = &&(); fn foo<'a, 'b, T>(_: &'a &'b (), v: &'b T) -> &'a T { v } fn bad<'a, T>(x: &'a T) -> &'static T { let f: fn(_, &T) -> &'static T = foo; f(UNIT, x) } fn main() { let r: &'static String; { let s = String::from("temporary"); r = bad(&s); println!("while alive: {}", r); } println!("use-after-free reads: {}", r); } ``` The only difference from that test case is the number of parameters and arguments in `foo`. title: `cargo install rust-update` fails, because linker not found.
body:
After successfully installing rust from `rust-1.97.1-x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm.msi` with `msiexec /I rust-1.97.1-x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm.msi TARGETDIR=C:\prgs\rust INSTALLDIR=C:\prgs\rust INSTALLFOLDER=C:\prgs\rust ALLUSERS="" /l*v log.txt`. rust was installed without mingw, because `msys` is in path. I tried this code: ```rust cargo install rust-update ``` I expected to see this happen: to install `rust-update` without hasles. Instead, this happened: ``` > cargo install rust-update Updating crates.io index Installing rust-update v0.1.0 Updating crates.io index Compiling rust-update v0.1.0 error: linker `x86_64-w64-mingw32-clang` not found | = note: program not found error: could not compile `rust-update` (bin "rust-update") due to 1 previous error error: failed to compile `rust-update v0.1.0`, intermediate artifacts can be found at `C:\Users\scth-muc\AppData\Local\Temp\cargo-install9QcQj7`. To reuse those artifacts with a future compilation, set the environment variable `CARGO_BUILD_BUILD_DIR` to that path. ``` Seems rust installs in a way not usable afterwards if msys, cygwin or mingw is installed sowwhere else. ### Meta `rustc --version --verbose`: ``` rustc 1.97.1 (8bab26f4f 2026-07-14) binary: rustc commit-hash: 8bab26f4f68e0e26f0bb7960be334d5b520ea452 commit-date: 2026-07-14 host: x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm release: 1.97.1 LLVM version: 22.1.6 ```

To reuse those artifacts with a future compilation, set the environment variable `CARGO_BUILD_BUILD_DIR` to that path. ```

title: rustc after 1.91 hangs during type inference case
body:
<!--
Thank you for filing a regression report! 🐛 A regression is something that changed between versions of Rust but was not supposed to.

Please provide a short summary of the regression, along with any information you feel is relevant to replicate it.
-->

If there's any more information I can give, I'm happy to investigate! Sorry for the length of the reproduction, I couldn't find anything shorter.

### Code

I tried this code:

```rust
use std::marker::PhantomData;

pub trait Marker {}
impl Marker for () {}

pub trait Relation {
    type Domain: Marker;
    type Codomain: Marker;
}

pub trait Follow<R: Relation, E: Marker, const DIR: bool> {}

impl<R: Relation> Follow<R, R::Codomain, true> for R::Domain {}
impl<R: Relation> Follow<R, R::Domain, false> for R::Codomain {}

// this bound on T is somehow important?
pub trait Container<T: Marker>: IntoIterator<Item = T> {
    type WithReplacedMarker<N: Marker>: Container<N>;
    type IDContainer;
}

impl<T: Marker> Container<T> for Option<T> {
    type WithReplacedMarker<N: Marker> = Option<N>;
    type IDContainer = Option<()>;
}

struct StubQueryable<E: Marker, C: Container<E>>(PhantomData<(E, C)>);

impl<E: Marker, C: Container<E>> Queryable for StubQueryable<E, C> {
    type Output = E;
    type Container = C;
}

pub trait Queryable {
    type Output: Marker;
    type Container: Container<Self::Output>;

    fn finish(&self) -> <Self::Container as Container<Self::Output>>::IDContainer {
        todo!()
    }

    fn follow<R: Relation, E: Marker, const DIR: bool>(
        &self,
        _r: &R,
    ) -> impl Queryable<Output = E, Container = Option<E>> {
        StubQueryable::<E, Option<E>>(PhantomData)
    }
}


struct R;
impl Relation for R {
    type Domain = ();
    type Codomain = ();
}

fn run_on(q: &impl Queryable<Output = (), Container = Option<()>>) {
    // this line causes rustc to hang:
    q.follow(&R).finish();
}
```

I expected to see this happen: Compile error due to inability to determine the value of the `DIR` generic parameter.

Instead, this happened: rustc hangs in a presumably-infinite loop (at least 60 seconds instead of 40ms)

title: cargo doc freezes on libc with nightly-2026-08-03
body:
Starting on the nightly build from August 3rd, 2026, `cargo doc` has been freezing when trying to build documentation for large projects.

To see this happen, try running `cargo +nightly-2026-08-03 doc --workspace --no-deps` on a project like rust-lang/libc. This is especially noticeable if the project has a lot of items that are re-exported or modules marked with `#[doc(hidden)]`.

It should finish without issues, just like it did on the nightly build from August 2nd. Instead, the `rustdoc`/`rustc` process gets stuck, uses a ton of CPU and memory, and is eventually killed after about 3.5 minutes with a SIGTERM signal (exit code 143). This problem is also causing the libc continuous integration tests to fail: https://github.com/rust-lang/libc/actions/runs/30800111327/job/91642485751

The documentation build worked fine with:
nightly-2026-08-02 (1.99.0-nightly, commit 73dc9167f)

The issue started with:
rustc --version --verbose: rustc 1.99.0-nightly (11177f223 2026-08-02)

I can't provide a backtrace because the process just hangs; it doesn't crash.

I suspect the problem might be related to pull request #159881. This change modified how the `visible_parent_map` uses a Breadth-First Search (BFS) to go into children of `#[doc(hidden)]` modules. However, it seems fallback items are never marked as "visited." This means they get added back into the queue from every parent path, causing a huge increase in processing, especially with libc's module structure. I confirmed this by looking at the nightly build manifests:
- https://static.rust-lang.org/dist/2026-08-02/channel-rust-nightly.toml (commit 73dc9167f, works)
- https://static.rust-lang.org/dist/2026-08-03/channel-rust-nightly.toml (commit 11177f223, hangs)

title: Regression: crt* Objects not found in library search path after #158823
body:
I faced a regression in building rust for l4re introduced by #158823. The core of the problem seems to be that FileSearch (from compilter/rustc_session/src/filesearch.rs) is used both to locate C runtime objects (crt*) and native libraries. However, #158823 introduces a prefix-filtering of the files found in the search paths (given by "-L" or "-Lnative") and this prefix only selects libraries and discards crt objects:

```rust
let prefixes = ["lib", &target.staticlib_prefix, &target.dll_prefix];
...
    if !prefixes.iter().any(|prefix| filename.starts_with(prefix)) {                                                                                                          
      return None;                                                                                                                                                          
    }                                                                                                                                                                         

```

A bit more detailled: My target config uses pre_link_objects to define the file names of the crt* files. These files are searched for in `rustc_codegen_ssa/src/back/link.rs` in `link_natively(...)` via `get_object_file_path(..)` which after the change uses `get_file_candidates(...)` which due to the filtering explained above only includes libraries.
